concepts.title: Homography
concepts.one_liner: A homography is a geometric transformation that preserves straight lines and maps points via a $3 \times 3$ matrix in homogeneous coordinates.
concepts.content:
Let's start with a formal definition of the homography. A homography (or projective transformation) is a geometric transformation that preserves straight lines. The homography is a function $h$ that maps points into points, $\mathbf{p}' = h(\mathbf{p})$, with the property that if points $\mathbf{p}_1$, $\mathbf{p}_2$, and $\mathbf{p}_3$ are colinear, then the transformed points $h(\mathbf{p}_1)$, $h(\mathbf{p}_2)$, and $h(\mathbf{p}_3)$ are also colinear. Such a function, $\mathbf{p}' = h(\mathbf{p})$, can be written in homogeneous coordinates as a product with a matrix:

$$\begin{bmatrix}    x' \\
    y' \\
    w' 
    \end{bmatrix}
    =
    \begin{bmatrix}
    a & b & c \\
    d & e & f \\
    g & h & i
    \end{bmatrix}
    \begin{bmatrix}
    x \\
    y \\
    1 
    \end{bmatrix}
    $$

This can be written in the short form:
$$\mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{H} \mathbf{p}    $$ where $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{p}'$
correspond to 2D points in homogeneous coordinates, and $\mathbf{H}$ is a $3 \times 3$ matrix.
concepts.motivation_md: Homographies model transformations between images that preserve straight lines, crucial for relating points across views in computer vision.
concepts.recap_md:
- A homography preserves colinearity of points.
- It maps points via a $3 \times 3$ matrix in homogeneous coordinates.
- Used to relate points between images under projective transformations.

concepts.title: Camera Rotation
concepts.one_liner: Camera rotation without translation relates corresponding image points by a homography represented by a $3 \times 3$ matrix.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding camera rotation homographies explains how images taken from the same point but different orientations relate via a $3 \times 3$ matrix, enabling geometric transformations without translation.
concepts.recap_md:
- Camera rotation without translation relates image points by a homography.
- The homography is a $3 \times 3$ matrix derived from camera intrinsics and rotation.
- Corresponding points transform via $\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{K} \mathbf{R} \mathbf{K}^{-1}$.

slots.motivation: Understanding camera rotation homographies explains how images taken from the same point but different orientations relate via a $3 \times 3$ matrix, enabling geometric transformations without translation.
slots.key_passage:
- Camera rotation without translation relates image points by a homography.
- The homography is a $3 \times 3$ matrix derived from camera intrinsics and rotation.
- Corresponding points transform via $\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{K} \mathbf{R} \mathbf{K}^{-1}$.

key_passage.text: The three images are taken from the same point by rotating the camera. There is no translation between the three camera positions as the photographer took the three images by keeping the camera origin static when moving the camera. Under this condition, the coordinates of the corresponding points across each pair of images are related by a homography independently of how far they are from the camera.

concepts.title: Planar Surface
concepts.one_liner: Corresponding points on a planar surface across two camera views are related by a homography.
concepts.motivation_md: Relating points on planar surfaces across views with homographies enables precise geometric transformations and simplifies correspondence problems.
concepts.recap_md:
- Points on a planar surface relate across views by a homography.
- The world coordinate system can be placed on the plane with $Z=0$.
- Homography is a stronger but conditional constraint compared to epipolar geometry.

slots.motivation: Relating points on planar surfaces across views with homographies enables precise geometric transformations and simplifies correspondence problems.
slots.key_passage:
- Points on a planar surface relate across views by a homography.
- The world coordinate system can be placed on the plane with $Z=0$.
- Homography is a stronger but conditional constraint compared to epipolar geometry.

key_passage.text: A second case is when two cameras observe a 2D plane. In that case, the coordinates of corresponding points across the two camera views, for points inside the plane, are related by a homography.

motivation.text: A homography is a stronger constraint than the epipolar constraint between corresponding points across two camera views. However, the homography only applies under certain conditions as we have seen, while the epipolar constraint always holds.

example.text: Two pictures of a building facade taken from different positions. The coordinates of corresponding points on the planar facade are related by a homography.

concepts.title: Direct Linear Transform Algorithm
concepts.one_liner: The Direct Linear Transform (DLT) algorithm estimates a homography matrix from at least four point correspondences by solving a linear system.
concepts.content:
### Direct Linear Transform Algorithm

Given a set of point locations, and their correspondences across the two cameras, we can compute the homography relating the locations of imaged points within the two cameras. To estimate the homography we can use the direct linear transform (DLT) algorithm, as we did for the camera calibration problem in @sec-camera_calibration. This will give us a linear set of equations for the parameters of the homography matrix with the form:
$$\mathbf{A} \mathbf{h} = \mathbf{0}$$ where $\mathbf{A}$ is a$2N \times 9$ matrix, when given $N$ corresponding pairs. The vector $\mathbf{h}$ contains all the elements of the matrix $\mathbf{H}$ stacked as a column vector of length 9. Note that $\mathbf{h}$ only has 8 degrees of freedom as the results do not change for a global scaling of all the values. Therefore we will need at least four correspondences to estimate the homography between two sets of corresponding points, as the ones shown in @fig-fig_matching_two_images. As before, the solution is the vector that minimizes the residual $\|\mathbf{A} \mathbf{h} \|^2$. The result is given by the eigenvector of the matrix $\mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{A}$ with the smallest eigenvalue.

In practice, to get accurate results, it is useful to also minimize the reprojection error after you initialize with the DLT solution since $\|\mathbf{A} \mathbf{h} \|^2$ is meaningless geometrically.
concepts.motivation_md: DLT provides a practical method to estimate homographies from point correspondences, foundational for many computer vision tasks.
concepts.recap_md:
- DLT estimates homography from at least four point correspondences.
- It solves a linear system $\mathbf{A} \mathbf{h} = \mathbf{0}$.
- Minimizing reprojection error improves accuracy after initial DLT solution.

concepts.title: Robust Model Fitting: Random Sampling with Consensus
concepts.one_liner: RANSAC (random sampling with consensus) robustly fits models to data by iteratively sampling minimal sets, computing model parameters, and selecting the model with the largest consensus set of inliers.
concepts.content:
To perform image stitching, we need to find the homography parameters that best describe the transformation from one image to another. Because feature point detection can be noisy, homography fitting must be robust against inevitable feature mismatches. A good algorithm for robust model fitting is RANSAC (random sampling with consensus) @Fischler1981.

The RANSAC procedure is simple and its name describes its steps. First, randomly select a minimal set of datapoints sufficient to fit the model parameters (e.g., line parameters, homography). Then compute the model from these points. Next, determine the inliers in the dataset—points fitting the model within some tolerance. Repeat this process $N$ times. Finally, compute the model from the largest consensus set of inliers.

@fig-ransac illustrates RANSAC for fitting a line to datapoints. Two points (minimal set) are randomly selected (green points in @fig-ransac (b)), defining a line. The number of inliers (points within $\epsilon$ of this line) is counted. This repeats for $S$ samplings. The final model is fitted from the inliers of the model with the most inliers.

(see figure: RANSAC applied to robust estimation of line parameters. (a) Datapoints for which robust line estimation is sought. (b) Two points (in blue) are selected at random, sufficient to estimate line model...)

@Fischler1981 derives a heuristic for the number of samples $S$ needed to ensure a good fit. Let $n$ be the number of points needed to specify the model, and $w$ the probability a selected point is an inlier. Then $w^n$ is the probability all selected points are inliers, and $1 - w^n$ the probability at least one is an outlier. The probability that $k$ trials select only bad models is $(1 - w^n)^k$. If $p$ is the desired probability of selecting a good model, then:
$$1-p = (1 - w^n)^k$$
Taking logarithms and solving for $k$:
$$k = \frac{\log(1-p)}{\log(1-w^n)}$$

For example, in @fig-ransac, with $w=0.18$ and $n=2$, to achieve 95% confidence, $k=91$ iterations are needed.

In homography estimation, eight equations are needed (four points, each contributing two equations) to use the DLT algorithm. Multiple random sets of four points can be sampled and RANSAC used to estimate the homography robustly.
concepts.motivation_md: Robust model fitting is needed because feature detection is noisy and contains mismatches. RANSAC provides a way to fit models by iteratively sampling minimal sets and selecting the model with the largest consensus, ensuring robustness against outliers.
concepts.recap_md:
- RANSAC fits models by randomly sampling minimal point sets and selecting the model with the largest inlier consensus.
- The number of iterations needed depends on the inlier ratio and model complexity via $k = \frac{\log(1-p)}{\log(1-w^n)}$.
- For homography estimation, sample sets of four points and use RANSAC to robustly estimate parameters.

key_passage.text: A good algorithm to fit models to data robustly is RANSAC, which stands for random sampling with consensus. The procedure for RANSAC is simple, and the name contains most of the steps of the algorithm. First, randomly select a sufficient set of datapoints to fit the parameters of some model. Then, compute the model parameters from the randomly sampled set of points. Compute the inliers in the dataset, that is, the datapoints that fit the model (or achieve consensus) to within some tolerance. Repeat that procedure some number of times, $N$. Compute a final model from the set of inlier points corresponding to the largest number of inlier datapoints.

motivation.text: Because the detection of the feature points can be noisy, the homography fitting needs to be robust against inevitable feature mismatches between images.

example.text: RANSAC applied to robust estimation of line parameters. First, a number of datapoints, sufficient to uniquely specify the model parameters, are drawn from the dataset. For this problem, that is two points. Two randomly selected points are marked in green. After finding the line that passes through those two points, the number of inliers (datapoints within $\epsilon$ of the model) are determined. For the line, the number of inliers is three. This process is repeated until some desired number of samplings, $S$, have been drawn. The output model is fitted from all the inlier datapoints corresponding to the model that led to the most inlier datapoints.

concepts.title: Image Stitching
concepts.one_liner: Using DLT and RANSAC, we can compute homographies between image pairs and align them with respect to a reference image to create panoramas.
concepts.content:
Using DLT and RANSAC, we can compute the homography between each pair of images and align them relative to a reference image (in this example, the middle image is chosen as reference). The estimated homographies allow warping all images into a single camera view, producing a panoramic image as shown in @fig-panorama.

(see figure: Panoramic image composed by the three overlapping images from @fig-example_three_images)
concepts.motivation_md: Image stitching requires robustly estimating transformations between images; combining DLT for homography estimation with RANSAC for robustness enables accurate alignment and panorama creation.
concepts.recap_md:
- DLT and RANSAC compute homographies between image pairs.
- Images are aligned with respect to a chosen reference image.
- Warping images using estimated homographies creates panoramas.

concepts.title: Concluding Remarks
concepts.one_liner: Homographies are important geometric transforms with many applications, including measuring planes, camera calibration, and neural network regression.
concepts.content: Homographies are an important class of geometric transforms between images with many applications. They can be used to take measurements on a plane given a reference measure. While we have focused on computing homographies using correspondences between images, homographies can also be computed in other ways. For example, to produce a bird's-eye view of a plane, one can compute the homography using the horizon line to determine camera rotation. For an uncalibrated camera, vanishing points can be used to estimate intrinsic camera parameters. Additionally, homographies can be extracted using neural networks trained to regress the homography given two input images @abbas2019geometric.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding homographies enables applications like plane measurements, camera calibration, and novel view synthesis; multiple methods exist to compute them beyond correspondences.
concepts.recap_md:
- Homographies relate images via geometric transforms with many applications.
- They can be computed from correspondences, horizon lines, or vanishing points.
- Neural networks can also regress homographies from image pairs.

prereq.rationale: Image stitching technique uses DLT to compute homographies between image pairs, so understanding the DLT algorithm is required to apply this technique.
The image stitching technique uses RANSAC, a robust model fitting method, to estimate homographies, so knowledge of RANSAC is required.
Understanding the DLT algorithm requires knowledge of homography since the algorithm estimates the homography matrix relating points between two images.
RANSAC is used to robustly fit models like homographies, which are estimated by the DLT algorithm; thus, RANSAC requires understanding of the DLT technique.
RANSAC fits homography parameters robustly to data with noise and mismatches, so understanding homography is prerequisite to applying RANSAC for this purpose.

overlay.rationale: Camera rotation homography is a specific case of a homography where the transformation arises from rotating the camera without translation, thus it is a special case of the general homography definition.
Planar surface homography describes the homography relation induced by two cameras observing a planar surface, which is a special case of the general homography concept.

Planar surface homography and camera rotation homography are two distinct special cases of homographies arising from different geometric configurations (planar surface vs camera rotation), so contrasting them aids understanding.
The concluding remarks discuss homographies and their applications, so they are topically related to the homography definition.
